questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: The state of nature as a measuring rod
questions.learningObjective: identify why an argument begins from a condition that never existed
questions.stem: A writer opens a case against inherited authority by describing free and equal people living without a common ruler. What is that description doing in the argument?

options.text: Setting a baseline, so any power in the actual state has to be justified as a departure from what people had before it

options.misconception: mistakes a measuring standard for a report of how people really once lived
options.text: Reporting a true historical stage, so the argument rests on how people really lived in the earliest times

options.misconception: reads a standard as a programme, which would make the writer a political reformer
options.text: Proposing a return, so the writer means to rebuild the old community as soon as the law allows it

options.misconception: flatters the new state instead of measuring the old one, which reverses the argument's aim
options.text: Blaming the present age, so the condition is named to make the new government look like a return to nature

questions.explanation: The described condition is a standard and not a report: because no government existed in it, every later power has to appear as a change, and a change has to give a reason, which is why the argument puts the burden on the ruler. The tempting answers turn the standard into a historical fact to be proved, into a programme of restoration, or into a way of praising a new state; none of those is what a measuring baseline can do.
questions.hint: Ask what the ruler has to prove, not what people once did.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: When a government spends its trust
questions.learningObjective: derive the conclusion that follows from limited, conditional government
questions.stem: A ruler breaks the law the people accepted when they set him up. Under the same theory of government, what follows?

options.text: The ruler's authority ends where his obedience to the original conditions ends, so obedience to him is no longer owed

options.misconception: turns a broken bargain into a private wrong, which the argument refuses to do
options.text: The ruler may be fined by the courts, but only for the harm his single act did to named individuals

options.misconception: assumes power cannot be lost, which the theory of consent exists to deny
options.text: The ruler keeps his power and the people gain nothing, since a bad ruler is a fact like bad weather

options.misconception: keeps the ruler in place and repairs the terms, which is a new bargain rather than a release
options.text: The ruler keeps his power, but a new ruler is elected who swears a clearer oath to the people

questions.explanation: If government exists only because people chose it on stated conditions, a ruler who breaks those conditions has used up the basis on which obedience was owed, so the people are released rather than fined; the argument locates the fault in the title to rule, not in the person or in one act. The tempting answers keep the ruler in place and attach a remedy to him, a fine, an unchanged right, or a stricter oath from his successor, and none of those is what makes the authority conditional in the first place.
questions.hint: Ask what the people gave, and what happens when the ruler stops giving it back.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: What toleration does not say
questions.learningObjective: distinguish toleration from approval
questions.stem: A magistrate allows two sects to teach publicly and tells each that it holds its own views to be mistaken. Which description of toleration fits that?

options.text: A legal permission that stands even though the state still claims its own belief to be the true one

options.misconception: reduces toleration to what the state cannot stop, which makes it a fact of power
options.text: A private tolerance, since the state only tolerates what it is unable to make itself adopt

options.misconception: assumes a negotiated neutrality, where the state simply keeps no opinion of its own
options.text: A settled compromise, since both sects agreed to call each other mistaken in the market place

options.misconception: confuses permission to teach with permission to argue, which are not the same licence
options.text: A licence to argue, since the sects may teach openly wherever they are strongest

questions.explanation: Toleration is a permission granted by a state that does not give up its own claim to truth, so a regime can protect a sect it believes to be wrong, and that gap between legal permission and private judgment is exactly what the magistrate is showing. The tempting answers move the state into a neutral market place where nobody claims truth, or reduce toleration to what the state cannot prevent, or mistake a permission to teach for a permission to argue anything anywhere.
questions.hint: Does the magistrate give up his own opinion?

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: The limit on holding land
questions.learningObjective: apply the limit that tests a claim to property
questions.stem: A person claims a plot in the common forest because he has worked it for years, though neighbours still hunt and gather there. Under the labour theory, is the claim sound?

options.text: Not yet, because the land he took is exactly the kind others can still use, so his work gives him no right to it yet

options.misconception: lets time of possession override the waste limit the theory sets
options.text: It is sound, because years of work make his title stronger than any untended piece of common land

options.misconception: calls common land ownerless, which removes the neighbours whose use bars the claim
options.text: It is sound, because a common is no one's land at all, so taking it injures no title whatever

options.misconception: invents a condition about company work that the theory never states
options.text: It is not yet, because the work must be done in company and his was done by one man alone

questions.explanation: The theory lets labour create a claim only against waste, so the test is whether anyone can still make use of the land, and a plot that neighbours hunt and gather over is still in use, so the years of work buy no exclusive right to it. The tempting answers say the long labour outweighs everyone else, that common land is ownerless, or that the rule requires company work; the first two erase the limit and the third invents a condition the theory never sets.
questions.hint: Ask whether the land is still doing work for other people.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: The reason to divide the powers
questions.learningObjective: state the single purpose the division of powers serves
questions.stem: A writer asks that lawmaking, judging, and enforcement be given to different hands, each able to stop the others. What is the point of the arrangement?

options.text: Power is checked by power, because each part can refuse the others, so no one part can act alone

options.misconception: picks a useful side effect and mistakes it for the design's purpose
options.text: Government is made slow, because every act must pass three desks, so despotism loses its speed

options.misconception: narrows the arrangement to one protection and leaves its mutual checks out
options.text: Rights are made secure, because a person is tried only by judges who did not write the law

options.misconception: leaves the ruler outside the arrangement, which is what the separation refuses
options.text: Government is made accountable, because the press may attend each desk and report what it finds

questions.explanation: The arrangement is built for one purpose: each part must be able to obstruct the others, so that no single part can make and apply a rule alone, and that is what turns a subject's obedience into a check on the ruler. The tempting answers point at a real side effect, slower government, judges kept apart from lawmakers, a press that may watch, but only the mutual refusal makes the person protected rather than merely delayed or observed.
questions.hint: The parts are separated so that they can act on one another.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: Reading law against the soil it grew in
questions.learningObjective: identify the comparative method behind a claim about laws
questions.stem: An original summary of a chapter on laws reports that in one nation the same rule on debt would be strict, in another lax, and that this suits the temper and the soil of each. What is the chapter arguing for?

options.text: That a law must be read against the circumstances of the people it binds, so a good rule fits and does not merely sound reasonable

options.misconception: reads a comparison as a verdict and picks the stricter case as the model
options.text: That a borrowed law is a sign of a weak state, so each nation should copy the strictest example it can find

options.misconception: assumes the variation is an illusion, which would leave the comparison pointless
options.text: That the variation in debt rules is harmless, since the courts in every nation reach the same result

options.misconception: reverses the method, replacing variation with a single body of law
options.text: That laws should be written by one body, so that a shared rule replaces the customs of separate nations

questions.explanation: The chapter sets two cases side by side in order to measure, and a comparison can only measure if the two cases are allowed to differ, so the conclusion is that a law has to be judged inside the conditions that produced it. The tempting answers read the comparison as a verdict, as a proof that differences do not matter, or as a call to abolish them, and each of those discards the very variation the writer needed in order to argue.
questions.hint: Why compare two nations at all, if the answer were the same in each?

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: The general will is not a count
questions.learningObjective: avoid reading a common will as a majority of votes
questions.stem: A community must decide on a common course of action. A thinker says the decision is legitimate only if it aims at the good of all, and not merely at the good of the many. What follows?

options.text: A bare majority can decide wrongly, because votes counted are not the same thing as the good of the whole

options.misconception: redefines the common good as what most people want, which removes the test
options.text: A bare majority is exactly right, because the good of all is whatever most people want

options.misconception: reads a strict measure as a veto, which would leave the community unable to act
options.text: No decision is legitimate, because any choice leaves somebody's interest outside the common good

options.misconception: keeps the counting and softens the test with a consolation rather than a criterion
options.text: A bare majority is a good servant, provided the minority is offered a share in carrying it out

questions.explanation: The measure is the good of the whole and not the number of wishes, so a decision that carries only because more people wanted something can be a decision of the many against the whole, and it is then not the will the writer means. The tempting answers either redefine the common good as what most people prefer, which removes the test altogether, or make any decision illegitimate, which would leave the community unable to act at all.
questions.hint: Ask what the votes are for.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: A contract with no government already there
questions.learningObjective: explain why the contract is not a bargain with a ruler
questions.stem: A contract is proposed among people who are leaving a condition in which no government existed. Why is the contract not a bargain between the people and a ruler?

options.misconception: puts a king in a scene that has none, turning the transfer into a purchase
options.text: The ruler is one of the parties and gains the right to rule, so the exchange is between parties who were equal before
There is no government above the parties to bargain with, so the terms can only bind those who make them

options.misconception: treats a king's consent as the source of the people's obligation to obey
options.text: The people had already chosen a king, so his consent is what makes the new terms binding on them

options.misconception: makes the ruler the subject of the gift rather than a party to a bargain
options.text: A ruler cannot consent, since only a whole people may give away liberty, and that is what the contract does

questions.explanation: The contract is drawn in the condition where there was no ruler to promise protection, so nobody can buy security and the terms bind only those who speak them, which is why obedience is not set against a favour already received. The tempting answers put a king in the room, make his consent the source of the obligation, or turn the ruler into the object of the gift, and each of those turns a surrender to the whole into a purchase from a sovereign.
questions.hint: Look for the ruler in the scene the contract is drawn in.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: The step after the first enclosure
questions.learningObjective: explain how a rule about property produces a conflict between rich and poor
questions.stem: A writer traces inequality to the first person who marked off land and said it was his. Explain how the writer believes the conflict between rich and poor follows from that step.

options.text: Once a share of the land can be held, some men gain a surplus and others none, so a bargain between dependants and owners is possible

options.misconception: shifts the cause from ownership to the difficulty of farming, which the writer never raises
options.text: Once land is marked off, farming becomes harder, so the poor are driven to the towns and turn against each other

options.misconception: runs the consequence into armies, which is a state story rather than the writer's
options.text: Once land is held, the owner must defend it by force, so every state needs an army and every army makes war

options.misconception: makes the quarrel a physical fight, so the economic tie disappears from the account
options.text: Once land is marked, the strongest man takes the largest share, so the quarrel is settled by a fight

questions.explanation: The step does not only take ground away, it makes land a stock that can be accumulated, so from one enclosure a surplus and a landless class both follow, and a poor person must then bargain with an owner who can refuse; the writer's charge is that the bargain and the enmity are the same fact seen from two sides. The tempting answers move on to farming, to armies, or to a physical fight, and each of those leaves the economic tie the writer is explaining unexplained.
questions.hint: Follow the step forward: what can now be held, and who has none of it?

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: What the target of the criticism was
questions.learningObjective: distinguish an attack on a church's power from a wish for its abolition
questions.stem: An author spends his best work on the records of a church that has wealth, troops, and a say in the law, and argues that it should be stripped of all three. What is the author attacking?

options.text: A church's political weight and its power to punish belief, not the idea of a god or of worship itself

options.misconception: widens a political complaint into a demand to end religion, which is a different case
options.text: Religion in every form, on the ground that any doctrine divides a state and should therefore be removed

options.misconception: names one order instead of the institution the author is describing throughout
options.text: A single order of monks, whose wealth one church alone misused and which should be dissolved

options.misconception: turns a complaint about powers into one about a profession and its pay
options.text: The clergy as a profession, since only paid clergy ever argue for a privilege they did not earn

questions.explanation: The complaint names three powers the church had gathered, wealth, force, and a voice in the law, and each of those is a political instrument, so removing them leaves an argument about a church's place in the state rather than about the truth of a religion. The tempting answers read the campaign as a wish to end worship, single out one order instead of the whole institution, or attack the clergy as a body of paid men; the text does none of these.
questions.hint: List the three things the author says the church should lose.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: Two answers to the same charge of illegitimate power
questions.learningObjective: compare two theories of when legitimate rule ends
questions.stem: Two original summaries meet: one says a ruler who breaks his terms forfeits the obedience he was given, the other says the citizen who entered the community surrendered the right to judge it alone. Which synthesis fits both?

options.text: Both refuse obedience to power that broke its own basis, but one keeps the subject able to judge while the other makes him part of the judge

options.misconception: makes the two agree on the ruler's power, which neither summary claims
options.text: Both hand unlimited power to a single ruler, differing only in the length of the term they allow him

options.misconception: assumes nothing can be restored, which neither account of legitimacy needs
options.text: Both begin from a contract already broken, so they agree that no legitimate government can be restored again

options.misconception: keeps the subject outside both, when one makes him a member of the judging body
options.text: Both leave the subject outside politics, since each believes law must be above his own consent

questions.explanation: The summaries share a premise and differ in what the subject remains: in the first the individual who has been overruled can judge the ruler's claim and act, while in the second the citizen is a member of the body that decides, so the surrender changes what the individual may do but not whether the community's rule is owed. The tempting answers make them agree on unlimited power, agree that nothing can be restored, or agree that the subject is outside both, and each erases the difference the summaries isolate.
questions.hint: What is left of the individual in each account?

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: Toleration offered as a limit on the state
questions.learningObjective: explain why toleration can be argued as a conservative position
questions.stem: A community is torn by a dispute over doctrine, and each side asks the ruler to settle it. Which course of action best serves the aim of quiet and order?

options.text: Refuse to settle it, because a ruler who decides a doctrine must enforce his own answer and becomes a party to the quarrel

options.misconception: hands the ruler the decision, which is the party-making the refusal exists to avoid
options.text: Settle it at once, because a disputed belief is the root of every disorder in a well-run community

options.misconception: lets numbers decide a question of belief, which neither side accepts as a test
options.text: Let the larger sect decide, since a majority faith has always kept the peace better than a small one

options.misconception: adds a learned body, which still has to return a verdict the state must enforce
options.text: Ask the scholars, because a body of learned judges can weigh the argument without picking a side

questions.explanation: Toleration looks like a concession and is not one: the ruler who is forbidden from settling doctrine has fewer quarrels to police and no opinion of his own to defend, so a limit on the state is a better route to quiet than a decree. The tempting answers give the ruler the decision, hand it to whichever side is larger, or send it to scholars, and each of those recreates the party to the dispute that the refusal was meant to end.
questions.hint: Who gets blamed when the ruler picks a side?

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: A church judged by ordinary rules
questions.learningObjective: explain what follows when religion is treated as an object of reason
questions.stem: A position holds that the marks of a true church are plain to any reader, and that argument alone settles which church is right. What follows for the churches?

options.text: Their claims enter the marketplace of reason, where they may be weighed and found wanting like any other claim

options.misconception: fences reason off so the marks can never be applied by anyone else
options.text: Their claims are safe, because reason can only examine what faith has already accepted for it

options.misconception: turns a test that can be applied into a grant of political power
options.text: Their authority doubles, because a church that meets the marks is shown to have a right to rule

options.misconception: assumes one test settles a competition, which is what two marked churches dispute
options.text: Their differences are settled, because two churches cannot both match the same plain marks

questions.explanation: If a church can be identified from marks that any reader can check, then the identification is available to anyone with the wit to make it, so a church's standing becomes a matter for argument and can lose that argument. The tempting answers fence reason off so the claims stay untouchable, treat a successful argument as a grant of power, or assume that the test ends the competition; none of them follows from a test that ordinary readers are invited to apply.
questions.hint: If any reader can apply the test, what is the church's claim worth?

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: How an idea survives a censor
questions.learningObjective: explain the mechanism that keeps a claim from dying in one country
questions.stem: One state bans a book and prosecutes its readers, while scholars in other countries go on printing, translating, and answering it. Why does the ban fail to end the debate?

options.text: Readers who disagree check one another's reports, so a claim that cannot survive scrutiny abroad dies there instead

options.misconception: assumes the rule travels with the book, which is the one thing a state cannot do
options.text: Foreign printers are forbidden the same, so the argument simply goes quiet in every country together

options.misconception: dismisses translation, which is what carried the answers across the border
options.text: Translation mangles the meaning, so the foreign answers are worthless and prove nothing at all

options.misconception: makes length the obstacle, where the exchange needed only a sheet to print
options.text: The book is far too long, so no reader has time to finish it and the argument never really begins

questions.explanation: The ban holds only where the state can punish, and the printed answer is the part that travels, so a claim has to be met in print by people who will check it, and a claim that fails there cannot come back; the censor's own order guarantees the foreign edition. The tempting answers assume the rule travels with the book, or that translation ruins the argument, or that length is the obstacle, and each of those is a reason the exchange would stop, which is not what a working republic of letters looked like.
questions.hint: What travels when the state controls only its own territory?

questions.topic: The list the books needed before the ban
questions.learningObjective: read a writer's strategy as evidence about the climate of argument
questions.stem: An original summary of a publisher's notice reports that a work was reprinted with a table of topics added, and that the printer was directed to name the writer of any article touching the church. What had changed?

options.text: Writers began narrowing what they would argue, so a promise of safety had already done the censoring's work for it

options.misconception: reads a list of permitted subjects as though the constraint had been lifted
options.text: The law had relaxed, so a list of topics was offered as a convenience to hurried readers

options.misconception: assumes the table is an apparatus for correction, which would not need an order about authors
options.text: The work had been found faulty, so a list was supplied to mark the errors and correct them

options.misconception: reads the order to name authors as the end of anonymity, when it is its beginning
options.text: The ban had been lifted, so authors can now sign their names to opinions they once had to hide

questions.explanation: A table of permitted topics together with an order to name authors on religious subjects are instruments of pressure applied before any decree, and their effect shows in the notice itself, because the subjects simply vanish from the printed work, so the climate and not only the law has been reshaped. The tempting answers read the same document as a relaxation, a correction, or the end of a ban, and each of those is the opposite of what a list of allowed topics does to a writer's plan.
questions.hint: What does the absent subject list tell you about the debate itself?

questions.topic: A motto withdrawn from a second edition
questions.learningObjective: infer an author's judgement of his readers from a publishing change
questions.stem: An original summary reports that the first edition of a work on the limits of reason printed an exhortation to dare to know, and that the second edition dropped it for a line of Horace about how little is known. What judgement does the change report?

options.text: The readers of the later edition could be trusted with the dare, so the encouragement was no longer needed

options.misconception: reads a withdrawn encouragement as an abandoned claim, which the new line denies
options.text: The author had abandoned his claim, and the new motto admits that nothing at all can be known

options.misconception: makes a publisher's substitution the author's, which the change alone cannot show
options.text: The publisher feared the older phrase, so a classical line was substituted to make the book look learned

options.misconception: explains a motto by sales, which no evidence in the notice supplies
options.text: The first edition was a failure, so the new motto was chosen to sell a second reading to the trade

questions.explanation: A motto tells a reader what to expect, and swapping an exhortation for a line about human ignorance withdraws the encouragement while keeping the same warning, which is what an author does when he thinks his audience has stopped needing to be dared. The tempting answers read the withdrawal as a surrender about knowledge itself, a commercial substitution, or a publisher's fear, and none of them explains why the second phrase concedes no more than the first did.
questions.hint: Compare what the two mottoes ask of the reader.

questions.topic: Freedom defined by what the state may build
questions.learningObjective: interpret a definition of freedom that licenses public works
questions.stem: A philosopher defines freedom as the only condition in which the welfare of the people can be advanced, and names schools, roads, and insurance as examples. What follows?

options.text: A state that is the condition of the people's good may set it up, since anything less would leave that good uncared for

options.misconception: treats the works as encroachments, which is the opposite of the definition given
options.text: The state is a danger to be kept small, since every public work is a new duty laid on the people

options.misconception: swaps the philosophical condition for the everyday sense of the word
options.text: Freedom means doing as one likes, so the three works are the limit beyond which no one may go

options.misconception: makes a philosophy of freedom into a pricing rule, which it does not mention
options.text: Public works are neutral, so any state may build them, provided it charges the cost to those who use them

questions.learningObjective: synthesize a claim about strangers with a claim about their law
questions.stem: Two original summaries meet: one argues a stranger is owed a welcome he does not pay for, the other argues strangers keep their own law wherever they travel. Which synthesis fits both?

options.misconception: denies the one duty both summaries retain, which is the point on which they agree
options.text: Both deny that any duty is owed, since each of them ends by sending the stranger home again

options.misconception: turns a duty of non-hostility into full membership, which neither summary claims
options.text: Both grant the visitor every right of a citizen, since a man is the same wherever he stands

options.misconception: makes the duty depend on a bargain, which is the opposite of owing it
options.text: Both limit the duty to a treaty, and agree that without one the host owes nothing at all

questions.explanation: The two summaries agree that the visitor keeps his own law, and that is what keeps him a stranger, so the one thing that does not depend on his law is the treatment he receives, and he may not be met with hostility merely for being unknown. The tempting answers make the summaries either abolish the duty or universalise citizenship, and both do the same damage, because they remove the distinction between the man who travels and the man who belongs.

questions.topic: What a general right still needs
questions.learningObjective: explain why a general promise of liberty is hard to apply
questions.stem: A writer objects that a constitution promising liberty to all leaves the judge with nothing to measure, since one man's safety is another's business. What is the objection?

options.text: A general promise gives no scale for weighing two claims, so a settling body is needed to make the promise usable

options.misconception: voids the promise, which is stronger than the writer's complaint about applying it
options.text: A general promise is void, since a promise to everyone can bind no one and settle nothing whatever

options.misconception: makes a statement of rights self-executing, which is what the writer denies
options.text: A general promise is harmless, because any judge can read a meaning into words that fit any case

options.misconception: supplies an appeal above every ruler, which no settlement in the case supplies
options.text: A general promise is enough, since a person may always take it to a higher court that no ruler can reach

questions.explanation: Rights are the kind of claim that two people can make against each other, so a statement of rights decides nothing until somebody says which right is in question and how much it counts, and that is work for a body that already holds the country's law and its customs. The tempting answers throw the promise away, treat it as self-executing, or pretend an appeal that reaches no ruler will settle it, and each of those avoids the work the objection is actually about.
questions.hint: Two men may hold the same right and still not be able to settle it.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: Whose rights the rights are
questions.learningObjective: identify the claim that a universal right is no nation's property
questions.stem: A writer is told that his list of rights is a novelty of his own nation and may be ignored as a foreign fashion. How does he answer?

options.text: That a right belonging to persons is no nation's property, so another country's custom cannot refuse it

options.misconception: answers a claim about ownership with a claim about precedence, changing the subject
options.text: That his nation has taught Europe everything it knows, so imitation is the proper form of respect

options.misconception: makes the claim depend on one country's courts, which is what the objection assumed
options.text: That the rights are enforced by his own courts, which no other state is obliged to obey

options.misconception: argues about the list's originality, which leaves the moral claim resting on a fact
options.text: That the list was borrowed from older writers, so its novelty is only a matter of wording

questions.explanation: The objection calls a claim about persons a piece of a nation's property, and the answer is that a right is not that kind of thing: it is held by the person, so a government that denies it denies something its own subjects hold too, and local custom is exactly what cannot settle the matter. The tempting answers appeal to a nation's precedence, to the enforcement of its courts, or to the list's own originality, and each of them leaves the moral claim resting on a fact the opponent controls.
questions.hint: Are the rights held by a person, or by a state?

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: Two different subjects in one constitution
questions.learningObjective: reconcile a universal statement of rights with a limited franchise
questions.stem: A new constitution calls certain rights natural, inalienable and imprescriptible, then gives the vote only to those with a stake in the land. Which reading holds the two together?

options.text: The rights belong to the person, while the vote belongs to the citizen, so the two rules answer different questions

options.misconception: turns a share of power into a payment owed, which puts the two on one question
options.text: The rights belong to the person and the vote is a reward, so the two rules answer the same question twice

options.misconception: calls the rights an overstatement instead of separating the two subjects
options.text: The rights were overstated, since a state that limits the vote cannot also promise what the person holds

options.misconception: collapses the rights into the vote, which the constitution separates on purpose
options.text: The vote was the promise, and the words about rights only described the vote that already existed

questions.explanation: The two sentences are about different objects: the first is a claim about the person as a person and admits no exception, while the second is about the share of power a citizen will exercise and admits conditions, so nothing in the first is contradicted when the second is qualified. The tempting answers make the vote a reward for rights, call the rights an overstatement, or reduce the rights to a description of the vote, and each of those forces the pair into one question and then must declare one half false.
questions.hint: Ask which sentence is about the person and which about the office.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: A word in a declaration that was read as a limit
questions.learningObjective: identify an internal claim produced by applying a principle to its own text
questions.stem: An original summary reports a woman answering a new declaration of rights: if the word used in its first line names one kind of person, the statement is a grant and not a claim at all. What is her argument?

options.text: The declaration's own words are broad enough to include her, so the exclusion is inside the text and needs no outside law

options.misconception: makes the wording a plot by her enemies instead of an argument about its reach
options.text: The word was chosen by her enemies, so she asks for a second declaration written by women

options.misconception: reduces the word to an office, which is a weaker claim than the text she is reading
options.text: The word names an office that anyone may fill, so she asks only that the office be left open

options.misconception: treats the wording as settled, which is the question she is raising about it
options.text: The word was never in doubt, and she objects instead to the penalties the state attaches to the claim

questions.explanation: She takes the word in the first line literally, and if the words are read as broadly as their logic requires, the exclusion of women shows that the statement is narrower than the principle inside it, so the fix comes from the text itself and needs nothing from outside it. The tempting answers move the problem to the enemies' choice of vocabulary, reduce the word to an office, or treat the wording as settled, and each of those gives the declaration a different subject and leaves her quarrel unaddressed.
questions.hint: She is reading the text as an argument, not as a gift.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: The emergency that undoes the right
questions.learningObjective: explain how a claim about the public's will can suspend the rights it established
questions.stem: A government at war argues that the safety of the people is the first law, and on that ground passes measures no judge may question for two years. Explain how the argument defeats itself.

options.text: The claim is a claim about what the people want, but nobody can say they want something else, so an unopposed measure stays unopposed

options.misconception: accepts the claim, which is where the defeat of the argument is to be found
options.text: The claim is honest, so a measure nobody may question is exactly what a frightened country requires

options.misconception: reduces the problem to a calendar, and the measure has no measure at all
options.text: The measure is only temporary, so the sole defect is that two years is longer than the law allows

options.misconception: attacks where the claim comes from, which leaves the claim standing where it is
options.text: The claim is borrowed from the church, so it loses its force as soon as a court reads it aloud

questions.explanation: The safety of the people was the ground on which the rights were granted, so a measure justified by the people's own interest is a measure the rights were meant to check, and once that reason is unlimited and unopposed the grant and its revocation come from the same mouth, so nothing in the argument can say which one is in force. The tempting answers accept the claim, make the trouble a matter of calendar, or dismiss the claim's source, and none of them meets the fact that the emergency has no measure.
questions.hint: What were the rights for, if not to check this reason?

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: What the comparison of women's faculties was testing
questions.learningObjective: explain why an observed difference may be caused by the conditions it is used to justify
questions.stem: A woman accepts that men's minds are shown to be the stronger, and answers that the women's minds were never given the same exercise. What is the force of the reply?

options.text: The difference was measured under rules that kept one sex from the training, so it is evidence about the rules and not about nature

options.misconception: concedes the finding the reply exists to put in doubt
options.text: The difference is real, so the reply only asks for more schooling and does not deny the finding

options.misconception: declares the sexes equal in fact, which is a different claim from the one made
options.text: The difference is a matter of custom, so the reply removes the comparison by declaring both sexes equal

options.misconception: refuses the weighing, so the conditions the reply names are never examined
options.text: The difference cannot be tested, so the reply ends the inquiry by refusing to weigh minds at all

questions.explanation: The comparison was made where one sex had schools, offices and wages and the other had none, so the gap in result is what those conditions produce, and the reply says the test was badly run rather than that the answer is agreeable; it accepts the standard and disputes the conditions. The tempting answers concede the finding, declare the sexes equal in fact, or refuse to weigh them at all, and each of those abandons the one point the reply was making.
questions.hint: What did the women not have that the men had?

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: A right that can always be set aside
questions.learningObjective: state the objection to treating rights as the ground of law
questions.stem: A critic says of a political theory that its rights may be set aside whenever a greater interest is alleged, and calls that an argument for something else. What is the objection?

options.text: A right that any reason can override is a convenience rather than a right, so it cannot be the ground law stands on

options.misconception: denies the objection outright, which is the strongest possible reading of it
options.text: The rights are true, so the objection fails and the greater interest must give way in every case

options.misconception: hands the right to the one who owns it, which is the opposite of a claim on power
options.text: The rights belong to the crown, so a greater interest may only be defined by the one who owns them

options.misconception: rules out the comparison, so the greater interest is never actually weighed
options.text: No reason is ever greater, so the objection is a complaint by men who dislike the existing order

questions.explanation: The criticism is not that the rights are false but that their whole force depends on being unoverrideable, and if a claim of greater interest always defeats them then the right was never a limit at all but a permission to do as one pleased until a better reason appeared. The tempting answers deny the objection, hand the rights to a ruler who weighs the interest, or rule out the comparison, and each of those restores the immunity the critic was attacking.
questions.hint: A right is a claim no one may simply overrule. What if any claim can?

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: Two sales at one printer's counter
questions.learningObjective: read revenue and reach as two different measures of a book's success
questions.stem: A printer's account for one week shows 1,400 copies of a six-page pamphlet sold for two pence each, and sixty copies of a quarto history sold for seven shillings each. What does the pair show?

options.text: The pamphlet reached many more people and earned less, since 2,800 pence is a smaller income than 5,040

options.misconception: ranks popularity by sales alone, so the dear book looks the popular one
options.text: The history was the popular work, since sixty buyers against 1,400 cannot be a wide reading public

options.misconception: invents a price for a sale the account does not record, and calls two totals equal
options.text: The two sales are equal, because a quarter sold at seven pence earns what a hundred sold at a farthing earns

options.misconception: uses price alone and so mistakes the cheap sheet for the profitable one
options.text: The pamphlet was the profitable book, since price and the number of buyers are what decide income

questions.explanation: Revenue is price multiplied by copies, and a quarter is eighty-four pence, so sixty copies come to five thousand and forty pence while fourteen hundred at twopence come to two thousand eight hundred, and the cheap sheet is the one that reached the readers who could not pay a quarter. The tempting answers rank popularity by sales, assert an equality of takings, or use price alone, and each of those forgets that who read it and what it paid are two questions with two answers.
questions.hint: Work out both totals in pence before you answer.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: Governments that began to count
questions.learningObjective: explain how making a social fact measurable makes reform arguable
questions.stem: Researchers begin gathering births, deaths, crime, and prices in a society whose rulers have never asked for them. Why does this change what can be argued?

options.text: A complaint needs a figure to stand on, so counting turns an old grievance into a claim that can be answered

options.misconception: makes the table an instrument of honesty, which is not what a number does
options.text: A ruler can now be shown to have kept his promises, so counting settles which side of a debate is honest

options.misconception: credits the count with administrative foresight, which is a different use of a figure
options.text: The people are described in numbers now, so a government can finally plan the schools they will need

options.misconception: treats a table as unarguable, which is the belief the count exists to correct
options.text: The old beliefs about society are settled, since a table is harder to argue with than a tradition

questions.explanation: The point of a number is that it can be checked, and a checked figure turns a complaint that was a matter of opinion into a claim another person must answer, which is what makes reform arguable at all; the ruler gains nothing by the count except an argument. The tempting answers credit the count with settling disputes, with planning, or with ending argument, and each of those mistakes a way of asking for evidence for a conclusion.
questions.hint: What can a number do that a complaint cannot?

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: The order that stopped the chairs
questions.learningObjective: distinguish suppressing a doctrine from suppressing the road to it
questions.stem: An original summary of an order of 1819 in the German states reports that the state paid for a chair of modern history and then required that the holder be chosen by a man loyal to the government, since in France that subject had overturned a throne. What was the reasoning?

options.text: A subject taught as fact can supply a young man reasons against his government, so the quarrel had moved from error to effect

options.misconception: restores the older charge about accuracy, which this order does not make
options.text: History teaching was inaccurate, so the state required a holder who would correct the errors in the lectures

options.misconception: makes the loyalty a matter of who sat on the French throne, which is not the given
options.text: The French throne had been overthrown, so the state required a holder loyal to the king who still sat in France

options.misconception: makes it a question of money, which the report does not raise
options.text: The state had no money for teaching, so the chair was kept but the appointment was handed to a loyal man

questions.explanation: The order does not accuse the historians of error, it accuses the subject of producing effects, which means the quarrel has moved from what is true to what a course of study does to the men who take it; a chair is dangerous because it hands a student the reasons that brought a monarchy down. The tempting answers restore the older charge about accuracy, or make the loyalty a matter of who sat on the French throne, or make it a question of money, and each of those misses the shift the order actually records.
questions.hint: Is the order answering a claim about truth, or about results?

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: A quarrel about where the ancient text was
questions.learningObjective: explain how a call to return to first principles can be answered from within
questions.stem: Writers are told that their laws are false because they are new, and that the only cure is to go back to reason as the ancients did. Explain the reply that was made.

options.text: Every age's customs are the ancient usage of its own time, so a return to reason is itself a new departure from what everyone then accepted

options.misconception: hands the contest to the oldest code, which accepts the challenger's standard
options.text: The ancients were the better judges, so the reply is to copy the statutes of the oldest surviving code

options.misconception: puts the answer in a later century, so the quarrel is deferred rather than answered
options.text: Reason changes from age to age, so the reply is to wait for a century in which it will be clearer

options.misconception: makes custom unjust until confirmed, which denies the one thing the reply relies on
options.text: No law is ancient, so the reply is that all custom is unjust until a court has confirmed it

questions.explanation: The call to return to first principles assumes that the ancients themselves began from nothing, and the reply denies it: for them their own customs were the ancients, so a fresh start is also what they would have called a return, and the quarrel cannot be settled by pointing at an age that did not exist. The tempting answers hand the contest to the oldest code, to a later century, or to a court, and each of those accepts that some point in the past is the standard the present must reach.
questions.hint: What did the ancients call their own customs?

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: An example used as a measure
questions.learningObjective: explain how a new example is turned into a standard for the old
questions.stem: An original summary of a later work reports that a writer crossed the ocean to watch a new republic, and that his question was not how well it was built but whether a settled old kingdom might be as free. What does the new example do?

options.text: It gives a measure the old world cannot answer, so a Europe that is less free now has something to be told about itself

options.misconception: turns the example into a plan to copy, which is not what the writer says he wanted
options.text: It proposes a model to copy, so the writer means for the old world to rebuild itself on the same plan

options.misconception: treats one example as closing the question, where it is meant to open the comparison
options.text: It settles the old question, since one free example is enough to prove that freedom is possible anywhere

options.misconception: rules out any comparison, which is the one use the journey was made for
options.text: It withdraws the question, since no example from another world can be applied to a kingdom at home

questions.explanation: The visit is a measurement and not a plan: the writer takes one society as the case of liberty and asks the reader to hold it beside the society he knows, and the value of the example lies in making the reader the one who is shown to be less free, not in offering a plan of government. The tempting answers turn the example into a model to copy, into proof that the question is closed, or into something inapplicable, and each of those removes the comparison that was the point of the journey.
questions.hint: Ask what the writer wanted the reader to measure himself against.
